clue.text: Terribly artful nation produces still-life painter

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly done, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A country with no artistic taste nonetheless turns out a painter of still lifes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terribly' rearranges the twelve letters of ARTFUL NATION into the French painter's hyphenated surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Fantin-Latour was a nineteenth-century French artist celebrated for his flower pieces and other still lifes.

clue.text: Writer-diplomat, whose early work had a certain aura

definitions.text: Writer-diplomat, whose early work had a certain aura

parts.words: Writer-diplomat, whose early work had a certain aura
parts.note: the Mexican novelist who served as ambassador to France, and whose 1962 novella is titled Aura

explanation.walkthrough: 'A certain aura' sounds like a vague quality of the early writing; it is the title of the novella Aura.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlos Fuentes was a Mexican novelist and an ambassador, author of the short novel Aura.

clue.text: Sensitive spot in Francis and Bragg

definitions.meaning: a tender place, as in touching a raw point in someone
a book title: Dick Francis's 1964 racing thriller has this one-word name, which the clue says Bragg also used

explanation.definitionFit: A touchy subject is a sore point, and the word is also the title of a Dick Francis thriller.

clue.text: "Glad to turn -.To stroll and teach from town to town."(Hudibras)

definitions.text: "Glad to turn -.To stroll and teach from town to town."(Hudibras)

parts.words: "Glad to turn -.To stroll and teach from town to town."(Hudibras)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Samuel Butler's mock-heroic poem Hudibras: the missing word describes a wandering preacher

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is the one that makes Butler's couplet scan and rhyme; strolling from town to town is its meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who strolls and teaches in town after town is a travelling, wandering figure.

clue.text: Kenneth, natural feature of French Without Tears

definitions.text: Kenneth, natural feature of French Without Tears

parts.words: Kenneth, natural feature of French Without Tears
parts.note: Kenneth is a character in Terence Rattigan's comedy French Without Tears, and his surname is a body of water

explanation.walkthrough: 'Natural feature' pretends to praise the play's naturalness, but it is a geographical feature that doubles as Kenneth's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A pond or loch is a natural feature of the landscape, and the word is also Kenneth's surname in Rattigan's comedy.

clue.text: Poquelin's imposter

parts.note: Jean-Baptiste Poquelin is the real name of Molière, whose comedy is subtitled The Impostor

explanation.walkthrough: Molière's real name was Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, so 'Poquelin's imposter' is the hypocrite of his famous comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Molière's play about a religious hypocrite who cons a household is subtitled ou l'Imposteur.

clue.text: Pound supports freehold possession for early dramatist

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece that supports another sits beneath it

parts.note: udal is the old freehold land tenure of Orkney and Shetland
L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Money props up someone's ownership of a property, for the benefit of an old playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'supports' puts L beneath UDAL. Nicholas Udall wrote Ralph Roister Doister, an early English comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Udall, a Tudor schoolmaster, wrote one of the first English comedies.

clue.text: Squaddies like Angelo

definitions.meaning: British slang for ordinary soldiers of the lowest rank
Angelo Maggio in James Jones's From Here to Eternity is an army soldier of the lowest rank

explanation.definitionFit: Squaddies are soldiers without rank, as is Angelo Maggio in From Here to Eternity.

clue.text: Associated with roses by Hergesheimer

parts.note: Joseph Hergesheimer's 1929 book about the American South is titled with these blades and roses

explanation.definitionFit: Hergesheimer's book of Civil War sketches pairs these weapons with roses in its title.

clue.text: Stuttering publication, aka Mr Porter

parts.note: the stammering publican of Finnegans Wake, who also appears under the name Mr Porter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Publication' hides 'publican': the hero of Joyce's Finnegans Wake keeps a pub, stammers, and is called Mr Porter in one chapter.
explanation.definitionFit: Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker, the innkeeper of Joyce's Finnegans Wake, stutters and goes by the name Mr Porter.

clue.text: Achebe's shaft from heaven

parts.note: Chinua Achebe's novel is titled with a missile of God

explanation.definitionFit: Achebe's novel Arrow of God names a projectile, a shaft sent from the divine.

clue.text: City in the best traditions of Ancient Greece

indicators.note: the city's name sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A city that lives up to the finest traditions of classical Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals the six-letter run within THE BEST; the rest of the clue confirms the city was Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Thebes was a major city-state of ancient Boeotia, rival to Athens and Sparta.

clue.text: Run-of-the-mill family in Victorian novel

parts.note: the family that runs Dorlcote Mill in George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss

explanation.walkthrough: 'Run-of-the-mill' looks like 'ordinary'; it means the family who literally run the mill in Eliot's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Maggie and Tom belong to the miller's family in George Eliot's The Mill on the Floss.

clue.text: Location of Zazie in New York?

definitions.text: Location of Zazie in New York?

parts.words: Location of Zazie in New York?
parts.note: Queneau's novel is Zazie dans le métro; an American would call the métro by another name

explanation.walkthrough: Queneau's Zazie dans le métro puts her on the underground railway, which New Yorkers call by a different word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Paris métro is an underground railway, which in New York goes by another name.

clue.text: Rainbow sisters who were in love

definitions.text: Rainbow sisters who were in love

parts.words: Rainbow sisters who were in love
parts.note: Ursula and Gudrun, the sisters of D H Lawrence's The Rainbow and its sequel Women in Love

explanation.walkthrough: 'Who were in love' sounds romantic, but it points to Lawrence's sequel Women in Love.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursula and Gudrun share this surname in Lawrence's novels The Rainbow and Women in Love.

clue.text: A loud, featureless American provides creative inspiration

parts.note: F stands for forte, loud in music
flat means dull and without features, like flat country

explanation.surface: A noisy, bland American somehow supplies the spark of creativity.
explanation.walkthrough: F is the musical mark forte, meaning loud.
explanation.definitionFit: Afflatus is a divine breath or impulse believed to spur poets and artists.

clue.text: Tennyson tells us that in their land it seemed always afternoon

definitions.text: Tennyson tells us that in their land it seemed always afternoon

parts.words: Tennyson tells us that in their land it seemed always afternoon
parts.note: Tennyson's poem about Homer's lotus-eaters has the line about a land where it seemed always afternoon

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek name for Homer's lotus-eaters, whose land Tennyson describes in The Lotos-Eaters.

clue.text: Angelic Spanish poet

parts.note: the Spanish poet whose first name is Ángel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Angelic' is not heavenly: it means having Ángel as a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ángel González was a Spanish poet of the post-war generation.

clue.text: Collaborator gets equal billing, or a touch wild

indicators.note: wild suggests disorder, so these letters run riot

explanation.surface: A partner gets top billing alongside the main writer, or nearly so in a wild way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges OR A TOUCH; 'gets equal billing' backs up the definition, since a joint writer is credited alongside.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint writer works together with another on a book.

clue.text: Elect Echo, so arbitrarily

indicators.note: arbitrarily means at random, so the letters are scattered

explanation.surface: Pick Echo, just like that, for no reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arbitrarily' rearranges ECHO SO.
explanation.definitionFit: To elect is to pick by preference, as in voting.

clue.text: Secret police's total lack of action

definitions.meaning: the Stasi was East Germany's secret police; add the possessive
a state of equilibrium or inactivity

explanation.definitionFit: The East German secret service with a possessive, and a word for stagnation or standstill.

clue.text: I advise no man to attempt opening this —— till he has my secret."(Rob Roy)

definitions.text: I advise no man to attempt opening this —— till he has my secret."(Rob Roy)

parts.words: I advise no man to attempt opening this —— till he has my secret."(Rob Roy)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Scott's Rob Roy: Rob's booby-trapped Highland purse

explanation.walkthrough: In Scott's Rob Roy the hero's purse has a hidden pistol mechanism, hence his warning.
explanation.definitionFit: Rob Roy's purse is the leather pouch worn at the front of a kilt.

clue.text: "It was like watching someone —— her own immortality. Every phrase and every gesture was studied."(Harold Laski)

definitions.text: "It was like watching someone —— her own immortality. Every phrase and every gesture was studied."(Harold Laski)

parts.words: "It was like watching someone —— her own immortality. Every phrase and every gesture was studied."(Harold Laski)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Harold Laski: the missing verb means to arrange or stage-manage

explanation.definitionFit: Studying every phrase and gesture is arranging and planning one's posterity.

clue.text: Zero gain recalculated for Miss Marsh

indicators.note: recalculated means worked out afresh, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: zero is the figure nought, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Nil profit after doing the sums again, as Miss Marsh discovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalculated' rearranges O and GAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Ngaio Marsh was the New Zealand detective novelist.

clue.text: Nothing follows a vote for son of Zeus

indicators.note: follows places the zero after the earlier pieces

parts.note: a poll is a vote or ballot
O is nought, nothing

explanation.surface: A ballot returns nothing for the god's offspring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follows' puts O after A POLL.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo, god of music and the sun, was fathered by Zeus with Leto.

clue.text: Hortensio found they would never hold with Catherina, though iron might

definitions.text: Hortensio found they would never hold with Catherina, though iron might

parts.words: Hortensio found they would never hold with Catherina, though iron might
parts.note: in The Taming of the Shrew Kate breaks a stringed instrument over Hortensio's head, and he says iron may hold with her but never these

explanation.definitionFit: Hortensio, disguised as a music teacher, has his stringed instrument smashed on his head by Katherina.

clue.text: Playwright from the plain, general public

indicators.note: from shows the name is taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A dramatist emerges from the plain, ordinary public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' points to the letters running across PLAIN, GENERAL. William Inge wrote Picnic and Come Back, Little Sheba.
explanation.definitionFit: William Inge was an American dramatist, author of Bus Stop and Picnic.

clue.text: 25's girl, asked to return

parts.note: the title of Inge's play is Come Back, Little ... — the girl asked to come back

explanation.walkthrough: 'Asked to return' is the title Come Back, Little Sheba by the playwright at 25.
explanation.definitionFit: In Inge's play the lost little dog is called back by name in the title Come Back, Little Sheba.

clue.text: Gaunt father of banished king

parts.note: John of Gaunt held a dukedom, and his son Bolingbroke was banished before becoming Henry IV

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaunt' looks like 'thin' but is John of Gaunt; his ducal title names him.
explanation.definitionFit: John of Gaunt was Duke of Lancaster, and his son Henry Bolingbroke was exiled by Richard II.

clue.text: Dreadful zone's sly hint from honoured writer

indicators.note: dreadful means terrible, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the possessive s counts as a letter here

explanation.surface: An awful, sneaky clue about an area, from a celebrated author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful' rearranges ZONES SLY HINT. Solzhenitsyn won the Nobel Prize for Literature.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was a Russian novelist and Nobel laureate.
